summary: Children calculate how long an event lasts from its start and end times by counting ON from start to end on a number line: first bridge to the next o'clock (a number bond to 60), then add whole hours, then add the remaining minutes. Make explicit WHY column subtraction breaks when the end minutes are smaller than the start minutes, so you have to borrow across the hour (e.g. 4:10 − 2:50). Time is base-60 (60 minutes in an hour), not base-10. Comparing two durations follows from calculating each; a later end time does not by itself mean a longer duration.
misconceptions: Uses column subtraction of end minus start, which breaks across the hour boundary
Thinks a later end time automatically means a longer duration
Works in 100s not 60s (treats the minutes as base-10)
Counts in the wrong direction or forgets the bridging jump to the o'clock

activities.title: Build the jumps on a number line
steps: Start at the first time (e.g. 2:50) on a blank number line.
Make the first jump to the next o'clock (2:50 → 3:00, a +10 jump) and say the number bond to 60 that produced it (50 + 10 = 60).
Keep a running total of the jumps to assemble the duration (1 hour 20 minutes).

Compare this count-on method with column subtraction: line up 4:10 − 2:50 and notice the minutes column needs borrowing, and that borrowing as if there were 100 minutes in an hour goes wrong, because the minutes are base-60, not base-10.
activities.insight: Counting on from start to end — bridging the o'clock, adding whole hours, then the remaining minutes — gives the duration reliably, and column subtraction misleads across the hour unless you remember an hour holds 60 minutes, not 100.

activities.title: Calculate then compare two durations
steps: Read a problem such as 'A lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00 — how long is it?' and count on to find 45 minutes.
Work a crossing-the-hour problem: 'A film starts at 2:50 and ends at 4:10 — how long is it?' bridging to 3:00, adding 1 hour, then +10 to reach 1 hour 20 minutes.
Compare two events, e.g. an activity from 2:20 to 3:00 versus one from 6:15 to 6:50, by calculating each duration (40 minutes vs 35 minutes) and only then deciding which is longer.
Test a tricky comparison: a 5-minute activity ending at 9:00 (so 8:55–9:00) versus one running 8:00 to 8:50 (50 minutes) — which is longer, and which ends later?
activities.insight: To compare durations you must calculate each one and compare the lengths; the event that ends later is not automatically the longer one.

checkQuestion: Set duration problems and WATCH the method: (1) 'A lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00 — how long is it? Show me how you work it out.' (2) A problem that crosses the hour: 'A film starts at 2:50 and ends at 4:10 — how long is it?' (3) 'Which lasted longer — an activity from 2:20 to 3:00, or one from 6:15 to 6:50?' Watch whether they count on (bridging the o'clock) or attempt column subtraction, and whether the comparison rests on calculated durations or on the later end time.
checkAnswer: Counts on 10:15 to 11:00 = 45 minutes; for 2:50 to 4:10 bridges to 3:00 (+10), +1 hour to 4:00, +10 = 1 hour 20 minutes; compares the two by their calculated lengths (40 minutes vs 35 minutes), not by which ended later.
